In recent years, extensive research has been conducted on the $\ell_0$ regularized least squares problem, especially under the assumption of Gaussian noise and a linear model. These studies closely simulated real-world scenarios where independent and identically distributed data is obtained through a linear process governed by an unknown parameter with sparsity characteristics. Notably, it was proven in theory that sparse priors lead to optimal estimation performance both when using an under-parameterized setting and, more significantly, when using an over-parameterized setting. However, our current work reveals different behavior in an over-parameterized setting under a linear time series framework with Gaussian noise. We demonstrate that, even with an over-parameterized setting, sparse estimation consistency is not guaranteed under general time series framework due to the presence of dependence in observed data, but is established when the data mixing rate is exponential. Furthermore, our results show that when the regression matrix is randomly generated from a Gaussian distribution and the level of over-parameterization is sufficiently high, sparse estimation at an exponential mixing rate is achieved, an over-parameterized setting leads to better estimation performance when there is weak mixing rate.

In modern peer-to-peer data distribution systems, storage providers are given incentive to share their storage spaces with the network. The decision to participate depends on their assessment of the risks and rewards. To address the lack of understanding about how providers evaluate and take on network risks, this paper develops a self-allocation decision model that takes into consideration risk avoidance. It aims to maximize the difference between utility gains and expected values of reward and cost. A numerical analysis of this model's outcomes is presented, and it is discovered that, in certain situations, providers are better off leaving the network. The natural outcome of this risk-aware self-allocation process in decentralized environments is that providers make informed decisions to join or leave the network.

A simplified computer model to simulate global atmospheric conditions was used to replicate the Mars atmosphere over the course of a year. This approach helped identify the various patterns and behaviors of the atmosphere, including the presence of turbulent weather systems, areas of strong winds, and annual wind currents. To further analyze these patterns, we examined the models' atmospheric features and compared them with those of the Mars atmosphere, using distinct patterns of wind and turbulence as organizing principles. This examination revealed that turbulence and large-scale wind currents undergo yearly changes, undergoing transformations throughout the year, including daily, seasonal, and annual cycles. This analysis also demonstrated that key aspects of the models' weather patterns are readily comprehensible even in more complex atmospheres, such as that of Venus.

Modern supervised learning typically involves updating model weights based on
successive batches of data, bypassing the recomputation-intensive gradient descent
algorithm's avoidance. Although this practice is common, several studies repeatedly
retrain neural networks, underscore the necessity of dynamic learning methods that
adjust the network's functionality beyond simple parameter updates. However, negligible
dynamic learning approaches are necessary given the substantial size of neural networks.
We investigate dynamic learning in a large-scale setting similar to Imagenet with
a million-class classification, demonstrating that even modest updates can greatly
improve performance. We discover that incorporating a classifier that distinguishes
between successful and failed image instances enhances the model's long-term
accuracy by removing its bias towards easily identifiable categories. Furthermore,
adapting the network structure optimizes performance, but merely adjusting the
learning rates replicates this success. This resulting dynamic network method yields
significant results by adjusting network structures in real-time during standard
batch-based learning. We implement this approach in a video content classification
task, showing that dynamic learning leads to noticeable improvements over conventional
methods.

Researchers have utilized the variational method with multi-valley effective mass theory and comprehensive configuration interaction to precisely calculate the ground and excited electronic states in silicon for various spatial arrangements of donor electrons. 
A detailed calculation of energy states yielded an accurate estimation of both intra-valley and inter-valley exchange coupling constants, yielding corrected values of 9.02eV, 8.65eV, 5.35eV, and 1.15eV at <110>, <-1-10>, <111>, and <100> directional planes respectively, with a corresponding spacing of $a/3$ between donor electrons. 
By utilizing a extensive, theoretically calculated dataset of exchange coupling constants, scientists have the ability to accurately determine the spatial arrangement of donor electrons in pairs or quadruples by analyzing spin-resonance frequencies and response phases. 
Furthermore, an exact method has been developed to determine the relative phase of the resonance signals in both electron spin resonance and nuclear magnetic resonance experiments, as well as in qudit systems employed in quantum computing. 
This analysis of the local electronic environment can provide valuable insights into the spatial arrangement of donor electrons in solid-state quantum computing experiments and other settings.

Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone. Both large and small size quantum dots, as well as high-quality quantum wells, showed evidence of the quantum Hall effect despite being outside the regime usually associated with this phenomenon, which typically requires stronger confinement. Notably, our findings are consistent with a theoretical model of a quantum dot's scattering states, demonstrating that the quantum Hall effect can manifest even in systems where this phenomenon is not commonly observed.

This paper investigates an advanced Time-Division Multiple Access (TDD) system, where multiple base stations manage multiple unlicensed frequencies to serve various users. To prevent interference between TDD bases, we propose a novel approach where they operate in a synchronized manner but dynamically adjust their scheduling based on coverage areas. This flexibility enables them to break free from conventional synchronization rules in certain scenarios. The problem of scheduling is modeled as a game among the bases to identify the most suitable configuration. Our analysis reveals that an underlying potential existence within this game. Moreover, in this paper, we develop a scheduling algorithm utilizing a projected gradient method.

Neural angle function differentiation is essential in various applications including human-like dialogue systems, where the accuracy of derivative estimates from an LMM directly affects the meaningfulness of generated responses. Our investigation reveals that Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) yield precise angle function derivative predictions, which are integral to the model and necessary for Hamiltonian dynamics preservation. A novel hypothesis posits that momentum variables learned by HNNs serve as indicators, providing a bridge between functional and differential information. To validate this, we developed a two-stage training framework for HNNs, incorporating functional and indicator variables in parallel. Experimental results show that HNNs are suited for neural angle function differentiation, with applications in enhancing autonomous vehicle navigation and packing efficiency.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient; it's crucial to also increase its reliability. We introduce a novel framework combining two innovative features: an adjustable score reflecting the model's confidence in its predictions and a method for data augmentation targeting areas of low confidence. Our first approach leverages special proxy samples to both score and target for augmentation, while an alternative uses actual user feedback for the same purpose. For the second approach, we integrate a simulation of a user providing feedback on areas of uncertainty to target for augmentation, again comparing this to directly using real user data. Our method is demonstrated through a text classification task, showing improvements in both reliability and accuracy when using our framework.

A newly defined polynomial, denoted as $\lambda$, is an invariant for links within the $T^2 \times I$ space. This polynomial builds upon the foundational $\tau$-polynomial from the braid theory of $T^2 \times I$. It is demonstrated that $\lambda$ retains invariance under a broad class of braid modifications, including the addition of full twists, right-hand turns, and strand crossings, as well as the reversal and taking of the mirror image. The polynomial $\lambda$ is shown to be more rigorous than the original $ \tau $-polynomial, and it has a similar relationship with the volume conjecture as the original Jones polynomial. The $\lambda$-polynomial is also connected to the original Jones polynomial, the Kauffman bracket, and the Habiro basis elements, den as $ \theta $, within the cohomology ring of the Jones polynomial.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a polysemous word based on the context in which it appears, within a specific domain or textual scenario. A significant body of research has been devoted to addressing the challenges posed by Word Sense Disambiguation.

This study formulates a genuine integral expression for the reciprocal gamma function, extending the properties of the classical gamma function. It also explores the connection to a previously defined, composite function, that of K. K. Stanciu. The study attempts to establish a, composite function, in terms of the reciprocal gamma function through differentiation, integration, and other mathematical operations.

The production of top quarks has been observed in experiments involving proton lead collisions for the first time, reported by the ALICE collaboration at the CERN. This finding relies on precise measurements of top quark decay into muons, accompanied by high-transverse momentum, and accompanying jets, as well as into electrons with the same characteristics. These observations were based on data equating to 11 nb of cross-section, analyzed into two distinct phases of the proton lead collisions, namely PbPb collisions with a transverse momentum threshold of 25 Geq/c and PpPb collisions with a threshold of 20 Geq/c, and into electrons and muons, respectively. The measured cross-sections for top quark and anti-top quark production, combined, were found to be 0.54 µb for the more intensive 2012 proton lead collisions and 0.14 µb for the 2010 proton lead collisions, respectively, measured at a nucleon-nucleon centrality of 8.16 TeV.

This study focuses on key aspects of understanding natural language for AI systems, specifically on a task called Cross-Domain Text-to-SQL. In preparing data for this task, researchers often use pre-made schemas and then tailor them to match the target database. However, there's a suggestion to instead use a universal schema that applies across different databases and to develop an extra skill called "auxiliary semantic interpretation." This auxiliary skill has two parts: identifying which table a word refers to, and determining the function of that word. An experiment was conducted to test the effectiveness of the proposed method, comparing it to other techniques and showing its benefits. An open-source dataset called T5SD was also released to support further research in this field. An analysis was also carried out on how different types of words impact the success of understanding text and on the value of the auxiliary skill.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within diverse network protocols and systems. As differential privacy gains popularity, the need to explain its nuanced application to network protocols becomes apparent. We first define differential privacy within the context of network protocols and systems, then explore various privacy loss accounting methods. Next, we examine a range of privacy accounting mechanisms, from basic bounds to more accurate compositions in dynamic networks. The paper also discusses core components of privacy-preserving protocols and systems, including efficient algorithms, cryptographic protocols, and graph exploration mechanisms. We then transition to an analysis of real-world protocols and systems that incorporate differential privacy, followed by an examination of crucial open questions and research gaps. Finally, we compare privacy loss accounting methods, discuss the effects of external factors on differential privacy, and investigate the applicability of graph exploration mechanisms to new protocols and systems.

The vast amount of images, data, and insights from the Euclid mission will be made publicly accessible, allowing research topics to be explored that build upon the findings of Euclid. This constructive approach will leverage the comprehensive information gathered.

A new formulation called the Phase-space Random Quantum Hydrodynamics (PRQHD) has been developed to address the time-dependent Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations within a framework that views the mean field as composed of a vast number of virtual bosons. These virtual bosons follow the Einstein-Tellegen equations and are given a uniform distribution in the phase space, except when an interacting component or an external trap breaks this symmetry. As a result, the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations are necessary to determine the quantum hydrodynamics of the condensate. A comprehensive set of tests has been conducted using PRQHD to solve the time-dependent Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations for a 1D Bose gas, comparing its accuracy and computational efficiency to the standard finite-element DFT approach. These tests included a static case with a trapped component or external trap, as well as a dynamic scenario with a sudden change in the weakly interacting gauge-invariant velocity field.

Given i.i.d. random variables forming a sequence, the Borel-Chebyshev inequality shows that the average of $n$ consecutive variables deviates significantly from their mean with a probability exponentially small in $n$. This result holds true even for sequences of correlated random variables under certain conditions, as demonstrated by Garsia-Rosevelett-Tewshamies and Guivarc'h-Tewaudren. However, we investigate the bounding methods of this principle and find that it can be replaced by a much tighter or less tight inequality, depending on the specific correlation structure of the sequence. Moreover, we find that the probability of large deviations grows at a polynomial rate in the number of variables for some short-range correlations.

We define a region minimizing surface within a homotopy class for any metric space, specifically a measure space, containing a given boundary. This surface has the property that for any function that equals one within the specified homotopy class and zero otherwise, the accumulated measure is less than or equal to that of any other surface outside the boundary. We establish the existence of such surfaces and provide a comparison with alternative definitions of surfaces within a homotopy class. Moreover, for Euclidean n+2-space for any whole number n, we prove that our surfaces coincide with 3-colorable surfaces that minimize area within the homotopy class, when considering surfaces with a fixed Betti number one under a (n+1)-dimensional Euclidean metric.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus have expanded, focusing on a rich structure of states with different stability levels near an energy state of 0+ at 0 zero spin. Based on results from previous research, a new theoretical framework was established to analyze a small cluster of states with 0+ stability, using experimental data from the 64Ni nucleus to fine-tune key elements. Notably, two previously unobserved states with 0+ were identified and labeled as 0+2 and 0+4. The 0+4 state shows significant similarity to the 4+4 configuration, indicating that a strong interaction between opposite-charged protons, including a component with no angular momentum, is an essential factor in shaping the 64Ni nucleus.

Machine learning models for natural language processing have seen significant advancements, largely due to the availability of vast amounts of data. However, effectively setting parameters for these models can be computationally intensive, especially when various validation methods are tested, such as cross-validation. In many cases, the stability of performance metrics during model evaluation is compromised, leading to suboptimal parameter settings and increased risks of overfitting. This issue is particularly prevalent in high-performance models, where even minor improvements in parameters require extensive model retraining. This research aims to address this challenge by introducing "fold jump" (JK) cross-validation, a novel, variance-reducing alternative to traditional J-fold cross-validation. By averaging performance metrics between non-consecutive validation folds, JK cross-validation can maintain similar or better parameter settings than conventional methods, while significantly reducing variance and lowering computational costs in certain scenarios. The effectiveness of JK cross-validation is demonstrated through various model parameter optimization tasks, showcasing its practical value in the field of NLP.

Distilling the knowledge of a large model to smaller, more efficient counterparts
is increasingly popular in the realm of artificial intelligence. Traditional methods,
however, often fall short in achieving efficient knowledge transfer. An instructor-
student learning framework has emerged as a promising alternative, where the
instructor adapts the data presented to the student based on its own internal
mechanisms, facilitating more effective knowledge transfer. Unlike conventional
approaches, this framework allows for dynamic interactions between the instructor
and student, enabling the student to learn from a diverse range of samples with
adapted difficulties. Although industrial applications of this framework are
limited, several academic studies have demonstrated its superior performance in
various tasks including machine translation, low-resource language tasks, and
natural language understanding. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of
algorithm innovations within the instructor-student framework and explores its
application to different neural networks. Furthermore, it discusses open challenges
and potential research directions associated with this framework.

We introduce a new efficient representation for functions defined on graphs, built using a concise combination of linear functions and modular components called generators that include additions, multiplications, and additions under conditions. This streamlined representation significantly accelerates the most frequently employed exact inference method, known as the message-passing algorithm for probabilistic logic evaluation, by a factor of three to twenty times. Furthermore, this enhancement facilitates a more rapid implementation of finding optimal solutions within specified constraints in graphical models. Experimental results show that our approach, integrated into the GAMP framework, outperforms the current state-of-the-art general-purpose method by two to eight times in achieving exact inference and finding optimal solutions under constraints.

Through a novel demonstration, an absorption spectrum of a single-beam light interacting with an ultracold strontium atom gas shows distinct asymmetries, indicating the impact of photon recoil on the Doppler effect for the first time. This influence becomes apparent under specific conditions where the speed of light is comparable to the thermal velocity of the atoms. These findings are essential for precise measurements using absorption spectroscopy and have a direct application in the steering of an ultracold atom beam.

When subjected to high stress, suspensions experience a sudden shift from shearing uniformly to developing localized flow failures, a phenomenon known as shear thickening. This transition is accompanied by distinct changes in flow patterns, stress buildup, and fluctuations, but extensive research on its underlying mechanisms remains局限 to a narrow range of conditions. We investigated the general principles of this transition by conducting numerical experiments across vast scales of inertia, gravity, and stress-thickening effects, utilizing a model that captures its non-trivial dynamics. Our findings reveal an empirical scaling law, demonstrating that combinations of these factors determine the behavior of the system, guiding theoretical and practical applications of the shear-thickening transition.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through a deformation of the Littlewood-Richardson algebra. A key property of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is examined, revealing it to be generated in degree two with relations emerging in degree three. It is also found that the corresponding Hilbert-Poincaré series for this algebra follows a recursive pattern similar to the Jacobi polynomials in the variable $n$. A special application of the resulting recurrence is discovered in determining the deformation of the Bondi-Metzner-Sachs (BMS) algebra from the Racach algebra $R(4)$.

An area where Web search personalisation effects have been studied in depth is how it influences an user's ability to locate specific pieces of information. This study breaks new ground by investigating how much relevant information might be missed due to the high level of Web search personalisation that occurs on Google. Our data, comprising 169 views of the same set of Web pages from one user over a six-week period, reveals how quickly relevant content becomes hidden from view and difficult to uncover, especially when considering the intricate relationship between previously searched terms and those with significantly different meanings. It also compares this finding with the rapid decline observed when Web pages are randomly altered, as seen in our control group. Notably, our results show a significant difference between human and machine-generated experiences when trying to break through personalisation filters, with former being much more stubborn than the latter. Lastly, our research highlights the design of experiments required to accurately assess the difficult-to-lose nature of specific pieces of information in the context of Web search personalisation.

To effectively advance our comprehension of the Higgs boson and beyond-standard-physics, a thorough investigation using a high-luminosity collider at 1 TeV is essential. This paper examines the feasibility of achieving comprehensive physics discoveries with a new generation of muon-hadron colliders, specifically exploring both proton-muon and pion-muon compositions. A successful strategy to reach this goal is demonstrated with a design featuring 10 ab^-1 of center-of-mass energy for a few distinct processes: a 0.3 MeV electron anti-neutrino branching ratio measurement accuracy, a 10^-2 cross-section precision for certain two-jet events, potential discoveries for dark matter models, and for certain supersymmetric scenarios with light squarks. These outcomes are realizable through optimized cutting parameters in analyses of specific electron-meson decay channels, certain electron-jet event configurations, and signatures characterized by missing energy and signatures within jets.

A novel method is proposed to advance free-breathing T2-weighted MRI scans in the abdomen and pelvis, ensuring consistent image quality and stable image intensity across breath cycles via a refined TSE sequence, then combining 3D MRI data from multiple diaphragm positions into a single, motion-corrected image.

The paired-permutation test is a statistical method used to eliminate possible cause and effect relationships between two variables. It involves creating a test statistic and determining the probability of rejecting the hypothesis that the variables are related, by comparing it to results from multiple data permutations. However, calculating this probability can be inaccurate when the test involves a large number of data permutations. In response to this issue, the paired-permutation test can only be accurate when the number of permutations is significantly large, which is not always feasible due to time constraints. Our novel approach, the paired-mixture test, mimics the test statistic's distribution by combining multiple independent and identically distributed components, by fitting the test statistic and its moments from multiple data permutations using the EM algorithm. This method enables the paired-mixture test to accurately reflect the probability of rejecting the hypothesis, by depending on the test in the limit as the number of permutations increases. The paired-mixture test only necessitates a relatively small number of permutations, which is more than sufficient for practical applications. This method outperforms the standard paired-permutation test by accurately estimating the probability of rejecting the hypothesis, while also significantly reducing the testing overhead.

A comprehensive freight rate index has been developed for the container shipping industry over the decade and a half from 1978 to 1992, supplemented by a year-long monthly average for each year, addressing gaps in the existing data records. These deficiencies adversely affected previous research on productivity advancements in the same industry during this time. Empirical analysis using RegDRIFD method reveals that total factor productivity grew at a yearly pace of 10.03 percent in the same time frame.

We establish an algebraic distinction between loom areas of torus surface groups, analogous how lengths establish the same for hyperbolic elements of the modular group. This is achieved by demonstrating that loom areas determine the veering triangulation of the torus, much in the way that lengths do for modular group elements.

The recent surge in using large language models for small data prediction tasks
has gained significant attention, with examples including the estimation of
financial indicators from news headlines and social media feeds. To address
the limitation of relying on labeled data in certain scenarios, we developed a
stock prediction system that combines BERT and GAN, and applied it to predict
company stock values based on press releases. The system achieved an accuracy
rate of 72% in predicting the direction of stock price changes for the NYSE.
Furthermore, we conducted an in-depth analysis of industry sectors, certain
company factors, and the recent historical performance of the stock market.

This research investigates the potential for detecting new physics beyond the Standard Model in Higgs pair production at TeV-scale $e^+e^-$ colliders, specifically ILC and CLIC.  To do this, we analyze the impact of Higgs effective couplings to electroweak bosons and top quarks on the cross-section for double Higgs production through vector-bosus fusion and top-quark associated channels.  By employing optimized selection criteria, we determine the sensitivity to these couplings and compare our results to those of other research.  Through a parametric study, we estimate the precision with which these couplings can be measured, even though their effects are generally considered too small to observe directly.  Consequently, we conclude that failing to account for these couplings in experiments could lead to misleading interpretations when searching for new physics.

We modify the conventional kinetic term in Kähler gravity and conformal gravity theories for Lagrangians that incorporate matter fields. A simplified two-component scalar example illustrates the reformulated kinetic term structure. In the context of conformal gravity, a transformation reveals an equivalent two-component gravitational theory with a specific hypercomplex Kähler geometry.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical object moving through a granular bed with fluid between the grains, considering both fluid that flows freely and fluid trapped within a membrane. The cylinder was moved in different orientations and speeds, as well as by being pulled towards the front, back, or sideways by attached funnels, to better understand the variations in drag anisotropy that resulted, especially in relation to the direction of movement relative to the cylinder's long axis, and the impact of added funnels, the speed of movement, the angle at which it moved, and whether the fluid was open or membrane-filled on the sources of the anisotropy that we observed, and the distinct drag patterns that emerged when the cylinder moved through open fluid-saturated bed and the one with a membrane.

In this study, we utilized a multiphase transport model to analyze several features of triangular flow in 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. By incorporating initial asymmetries and elliptical and triangular fluctuations in the model, we were able to replicate triangular flow, particle number, and $p_T$-dependent flow coefficients observed experimentally. We found that initial asymmetries significantly influenced triangular flow, whereas nuclear glasma initial conditions had negligible impact. Furthermore, we examined the correlations between elliptical and triangular flow, discovering that their interaction could be described by a superposition principle. We also found that initial asymmetries affected the midrapidity particle multiplicity but had negligible influence on transverse momentum-dependent coefficients or particle multiplicity differential flow moments. Finally, our results showed that the phase space density affected differential coefficients but had negligible effect on differential flow moments, which remained largely constant as the beam energy remained constant.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved several significant accomplishments in measuring rare decays and instances of charge-parity violation in mesons such as B-s, D-s, and K. In 2011-2015, the researcher measured the difference in decay rates for the opposite charge mesons to violate CP, specifically in the B-s-to-D-s-D-s pair decay. In 2014-2015, they directly counted the B-s-to-K-K bar pair decay to violate CP in this process. Additionally, the ATLAS collaboration first directly measured two suppression factors in 2015 for the D-s-meson's semi-leptonic decay to an electron and a anti-muon, and for the K's three-body decay into an electron (an anti-muon) and a neutral neutrino (an anti-muon neutrino).

The numerical solution of large-scale discretized HPMc problems using iterative methods like GMRES typically requires a preconditioner to improve convergence. For iterative methods to successfully preserve certain properties of the original system, three key conditions must be met: the initial guess should satisfy the constraints, the preconditioned operator must preserve those properties, and the search space must maintain a specific configuration. Despite its importance in various fields, research into Krylov subspace methods for HPMc systems with the purpose of preserving a particular header remains limited. This limitation is addressed by introducing a modified version of the PHASTA preconditioner that preserves the header of the system, thereby enabling property preservation in KRYLOV methods for solving large-scale discretized HPMc systems.

A critical step in image-guided surgery is achieving volume to surface alignment.
Knowing the precise deformability of a tissue can substantially enhance this process by leveraging a biomechanical model to pinpoint initial transformations and
remove rigid degrees of freedom from an optimization approach to determine
deformable parameters.
However, employing such a model often calls for computationally expensive simulations.
We present a novel approach to guide deformable alignment that excludes
birefracture and tension violations while significantly accelerating computation
time.
We exclude computations involving a model's inverse by utilizing a
mathematical formula to describe its behavior.
Moreover, we employ aneural network to expedite solving a system of linear equations at each
optimization step.
Evaluations on two distinct datasets demonstrate that this method
outperforms existing techniques with comparable alignment accuracy, but with
computation times nearly three orders of magnitude faster.

Self-supervised scene flow estimation poses a difficult challenge due to ambiguity in motion signals. Successful approaches in this field often rely on geometric and photometric consistency checks, utilizing auxiliary data such as depth and normal vectors. Recently, learned metrics have been employed to optimize these consistency losses by training neural networks. However, our research reveals that the complex geometric checks inherent in this approach present a significant risk for the effectiveness of such methods. We contend that even simple checks on flow and intensity consistency are notoriously difficult for models to master in real-world applications, given the intricate nature of geometric validations. In recent years, neural network classifiers using fully connected architectures have been highly effective across various tasks. However, the rapid advancement of neural coding research points towards spiking neural networks as the most promising way to emulate biologically realistic classification systems. In this paper, we take on a classic fully connected neural network and transform it into a random neural network using techniques like weight quantization and memristor-based circuitry, which simulate the electrical characteristics of real biological systems. We evaluate these networks across four distinct datasets, observing that they perform comparably to traditional fully connected networks while using significantly less energy, achieving results with accuracy rates of 92.7%, 94.3%, 94.5%, and 94.5%, respectively, and at the cost of reduced consumption by seven orders of magnitude. In contrast, they outperform standard fully connected networks by seven times, and operate with seven orders of magnitude greater efficiency than a single synapse. These results highlight the potential of spiking random neural networks to deliver both high performance and energy efficiency in classification systems.

The impact of a non-zero magnetic field on the thermodynamic properties of a spin-polarized strange quark star is investigated in this study, which considers a non-Abraja-mpland plasma at finite temperature. The equation of motion for quark gluon plasma is solved using a perturbative approach within the leading logarithmic approximation. The temperature and magnetic field's dependence of specific heat, pressure, and energy density is explored for both non-thermal and fully non-dimensional cases. The influence of the magnetic field on phase transitions is also examined, along with the determination of critical temperature in a non-thermal context. The effect of temperature on the critical magnetic field is found to be inverse, and the behavior of quark stars is analyzed in a non-thermal setting.

A perfect matching in a graph that can be decomposed into three independent matchings is known as an ideal matchings. The question of whether every cubic bridgeless graph contains an ideal matchings was posed by Fukshansky and Vanhove. The current research demonstrates that every cubic graph, free of $K_{3,3}$ as a minor, has an ideal matchings. Moreover, if the graph does not have a specific five-cut, then its ideal matchings are 3-colorable; however, if the graph does have a specific scenario with nine independent edges crossing a cycle of length eight, then its ideal matchings may not be 3-colorable. The paper also provides an efficient algorithm with a time complexity of $O(m^{1.48})$, where $m$ represents the number of edges in the graph, to find ideal matchings, Hamiltonian cycles, and a specific type of edge-coloring (known as a 3-factor) in cubic graphs.

Containerized microservices offer considerable flexibility and ease of management, but also introduce significant security risks in terms of system stability and privacy. Previous research highlighted the effectiveness of treating system calls as sensitive indicators and applying reinforcement learning to design optimal container call policies, but these approaches were limited to static systems where individual programs were interconnected. This research presents a novel reinforcement learning approach tailored for an autonomous OS-level container call policy learning system, known as Timeloops, which can dynamically learn optimal calling strategies in a broad range of microservices environments, regardless of whether they are statically linked or completely decoupled. We evaluated Timeloops on various test systems, including the RecSys framework, Okappc, and a custom-built statically coupled system, and found that it could successfully enhance system performance by reducing CPU usage and improving system responsiveness.

A starting point for trajectories in filtering applications is often modeled using a probability density function, but this can be computationally intensive. A new approach proposes discretizing the possible starting points on a grid to improve efficiency. A method is presented to integrate a partially grid-based starting point model in the Probabilistic Multiple Birth Filter (PMBM) without significantly compromising accuracy. As evidence, simulation results show that this approach can lower memory usage and processing time while processing new data. A particular scenario of a single starting point is also explored in the paper's conclusion.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes a decay term in its interior, mathematically represented as $u_t = \Delta w(\cdot,u) + f + v\cdot\chi_{\omega}$ in a domain $\Omega$ over the time period $(0,T)$. Here, $w$ is defined by $w = v(u)$ in the domain, and $w = 0$ on the boundary of the domain. The function $u$ must be non-negative, and it is required to reach zero at a specific point in time $T$, within a sub-region of the domain defined as $x_0$. The question arises as to whether a control function can be found to guide the solution to zero within the specified tolerance, under the condition that the population function $v$ is positive and continuous. It is demonstrated that such a control indeed exists. Furthermore, an explicit form of this control is not derived.

The enthusiasm of fans is heavily influenced by players' actions on the soccer field, which also holds true. High-value actions taken during crucial game moments can lead to increased team success, yet taking risks often results in negative consequences. The urgency to score during a soccer match is strongly linked to the current scoreline, but equally, the value of defensive actions becomes paramount when the team is leading or defending a goal. Reinforcement learning models have demonstrated significant advances in various strategic games, but their ability to fully capture the nuance of timely decision-making remains limited. We address this issue by creating a new dataset, soccer3d, consisting of professional matches with actions tagged for high-value and risk-assessed moments. Then, through a reinforcement learning approach, we trained an agent to make better choices in situations requiring both offensive and defensive actions, demonstrating its effectiveness with statistical significance when compared to an existing baseline.

Recent observations by the Very Large Array between 2013 and 2014 of Cygnus X towards the far-side have been reviewed. The dataset has been re-analyzed using the EMISSION inversion technique to address source modeling challenges associated with extended structures. The study explored various input signal specifications, including amplitude and phase, both from actual data and synthesized examples. The findings revealed that in order to accurately model extended structures, precise measurement of individual brightness features is crucial, which in turn necessitates an input signal with phase and amplitude variability on an angular scale smaller than the resolution limit. The current Very Large Array dataset resolution limit is approximately 7 milliseconds, corresponding to an angular scale of 40 micro-arcseconds at the telescope's location, which was found to be inadequate for accurately modeling the Cygnus X extent. The study also compared results obtained from the EMISSION technique with traditional fitting methods, such as cleaning, and found that for compact sources, the very high very high sensitivity of the Very Large Array allowed the detection of millisecond variability in the O435 line of the Tcn I at angular scales as small as the resolution limit. The investigation of source structures on smaller angular scales, however, is limited by factors including angular smearing, leakage, and scattering effects.

A novel stochastic differential equation model was developed to simulate political competition between a stable party and one that colonizes new areas. The stable party has an edge in overcoming minor random disturbances, while the party that colonizes new areas excels at expanding its reach over geographical space. The balance of success between the two parties depends on comparing the intensity of random noise in the model to the tradeoff of colonization abilities. The model demonstrates the possibility of sudden political shifts with no change in the tradeoff conditions, as well as a range of outcomes including the exclusion of one party, the coexistence of both parties within a limited area, or with both parties sharing the available space. The model also has more broad applicability than just to biological interactions, showing potential to describe various economic and social competition scenarios.

This research considers a new hybrid network that combines D2D data transmission and D2D power transmission, coexisting with cognitive radios and C-RSRs, where D2D links use an reflecting surface to boost their transmission power in the silent frequency band. An joint optimization problem is formulated to maximize the total network throughput by fine-tuning transmission parameters and reflecting surface configuration, subject to various constraints on transmit power, interference levels, and circuit power. By linearizing nonconvex problems and utilizing fractional programming techniques, an effective algorithm is proposed to obtain an optimal solution. Furthermore, an outer packing method is employed to accurately determine the optimal reflecting surface configuration. The proposed algorithm is shown to significantly cut computational costs compared to existing methods. Key performance indicators are analyzed to evaluate this integrated D2D data and energy networking system.

The demand for LDV systems is increasing in various applications, such as measuring fluids, structures, and electrical systems at a distance. The primary advantage of these systems is their ability to obtain simultaneous, multi-point data in real-time, including both local and remote measurements. However, achieving LDV operations over long distances poses technical challenges, mainly due to the need to align laser beams precisely to a single photodetector. Although feasible, this requires developing innovative beam-combining methods. The author presents a low-cost beam-combining method that uses a combiner plate to align local and remote laser beams to a single photodetector with high precision. The system's capabilities are demonstrated by acquiring complex, two-dimensional flow patterns at a distance, such as flow around an airfoil. The LDV system successfully captures flow data on a 400mm x 400mm measurement plane located 800mm away from the system, including flow fields both before and after a NACA0012 airfoil at a chord length of 200mm, with a free-stream velocity of 9.58 m/s. The results obtained using the LDV system show its effectiveness in acquiring intricate flow patterns in model aerodynamics applications, even over long measurement distances.

The complex phase plates used in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs) can act like an aberration corrector, countering the excessive bending of electrons caused by their design, a concept that was recently demonstrated with a successful experiment, allowing for straight electrons to be produced even when the device is imperfectly aligned.

We examine the spectral and orbital stability of small amplitude solitary waves in a relativistic field, governed by the anharmonic Klein-Gordon equation in one dimension. Our research proves the absolute spectral stability in this context and, consequently, establishes the orbital stability for solitary waves with a total energy level close to that of the linear solitary wave.

In recent years, researchers have broadened various number theory concepts using modular and non-commutative elements. This study develops the theory of Leopoldt numbers in non-commutative settings by defining a new number field ratio for a specific type of non-commutative element, a polynomial in an imaginary quadratic number field. This extension allows previous Leopoldt proportionality results to be applied to non-commutative elements, providing a generalised form of the theorem.

In environments with broken parity, the decay of a $B$ meson can lead to the dislocation of another $B$ meson through axion-like particle emission, and this process is highly sensitive to a specific type of interaction between the axion-like particle and the strong force. With the anticipation of Belle II's ability to collect a 10^12 $J/\psi$ cross section, a thorough analysis of various axion-like particle interactions reveals that this antenna source could potentially explore regions of hidden matter parameter space that were previously inaccessible.

Semantic alteration detection has seen significant interest from the research community in recent years. If we can identify instances where the meaning of a text remains unchanged and when it changes, we can provide a comprehensive understanding of the factors that influence how language is used and interpretation. In this research, we investigate the performance of contextualized language models on altered semantics and find that they outperform non-contextualized models. We release four newly created datasets in this research, two at the sentence level and two at the paragraph level, and observe that the effectiveness of models can be highly algorithm-dependent and prone to overfitting. Additionally, we provide a set of recommendations based on our findings.

During a period when scalar, vector, and tensor forces were unified, Quasars experienced a period where their superradiance could amplify signals, potentially pointing to a period where the universe's fundamental forces were in a state of transition. This paper delves into the features of the superradiance phenomenon in heavy quasar systems to identify the most suitable quasar for investigating the superradiance phenomenon, as the lack of electromagnetic charge in ultralight particles can lead to the collapse of bound states in heavy binary systems. By combining theoretical calculations with observational astrophysics, we determine the optimal heavy quasar system for detecting the superradiance phenomenon. Moreover, we determine the mass range of ultralight particles that could cause a measurable shift in the spin precession of heavy quasar systems. If ultralight bosons were to accumulate in the minuscule distance between the stars, their gravitational influence could cause the eventual destruction of the binary system. Moreover, if they were densely packed, they could give rise to a boson star within the binary system, with a minimum mass threshold of about $10^{-22}$ times the mass of the universe.

A distinctive feature of neural tissue development involves the migration of nuclei between the apical and basal surfaces of a developing sphere both during interphase and throughout cell division, occurring without the formation of a cell barrier. Although interphase nuclear movements (INM) has been observed in various systems, its role remains unclear, especially regarding its origin. Through mathematical modeling and experimental observations undertaken with zebrafish, we offer a zebrafish-specific investigation of the mechanism behind INM, leveraging easily measurable parameters for our model's validation. Our findings suggest that retinal INM serves a functional purpose by facilitating the access of nuclei to nutrients and oxygen at the retinal periphery during feeding intervals. Furthermore, we conclude that a diffusive mechanism effectively enables neurons to remain close to the retinal margin for sustained periods, thereby ensuring efficient access to essential nutrients and oxygen.

In complex visual task applications, such as video compressed sensing recovery and color image mosaic conversion, code generation that facilitates efficient and accurate recovery through generic, recovery-oriented optimally efficient code generation is frequently overlooked. We address this issue by creating a code generation technique that facilitates efficient and accurate compressed video recovery through a GPCR-OSC approach. The GPCR-OSC approach combines generalised oscillatory correlation spectroscopy with a five-point efficient filter to create a code generation technique that facilitates efficient and accurate compressed video recovery through a non-negative least squares approach. We evaluate the GPCR-OSC approach in comparison to existing code generation approaches, including code generation techniques that facilitate efficient and accurate color image mosaic conversion through a GPCR-OSC approach. We further develop a code generation framework applicable to a wide range of efficient video compressed sensing recovery techniques, including a code generation framework applicable to efficient algorithms that facilitate efficient video compressed sensing recovery through a GPCR-OSC approach. Experimental evaluation demonstrates the GPCR-OSC approach and code framework's efficacy in facilitating efficient and accurate video compressed sensing recovery through a code framework that facilitates efficient and accurate video compressed sensing recovery through a GPCR-OSC approach.

This study examines the effects of localized shape defects on interfacial dynamics in polar active fluids confined to $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ can range from 2 to 5 or 6. These defects, which are randomly distributed and immovable, take the form of point defects with a dipole orientation parallel to a local interface, and function as catalytic sites that enhance local fluid activity. As a result, interfaces between fluid and vacuum move towards regions with defects, leading to sticking behavior when two interfaces come into contact. This results in a self-lubricating mechanism that eventually causes interfaces to become blocked by shape defects, separating into independent segments or "gliders" that move at different speeds. Simulation data reveals that the movement speeds of these gliders follow a power-law distribution, and for 2-, 3-, and 4-dimensional space, we observe a range of exponents alpha that can range from 1.55 to 2.00, depending on the spatial configuration. Additionally, simulation results show that the average speed of these gliders scale linearly with the activity level of the fluid, and also scale linearly with the power of fluid speed limitation and fluid viscosity. Furthermore, there is also a linear relationship between the fluid's activity level and this viscosity-power-product. The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how transactions take place, with an increase in identity fraud risks due to the ease of sharing personal information, including Indonesian national ID cards. To mitigate risks associated with identity fraud, an Indonesian ID card data extractor was developed utilizing OCR and NLP techniques via Python on Windows 10. The extracted information from the ID card comprises the holder's name, gender, date of birth, ID number, and validity period. An ensemble method was employed to enhance accuracy in classifying gender information from the ID card, with testing conducted using 50 ID cards yielding a 96% accuracy rate.

Our introductory tutorial on applying Markov chain Monte Carlo (MC) simulation to solve the driven quantum harmonic oscillator begins by deriving the path integral expression for the propagator. We then introduce the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm and other essential concepts. Subsequently, we solve the driven quantum harmonic oscillator as a practical application, also exploring related topics such as expectation values, quantum states other than the ground state, and various collapse time observations.

The YORP effect's impact on asteroids is characterized by a torque that causes a change in their rotation speed over time. Observationally, this is represented as a rate of variation in periods per day. By analyzing light curves of asteroids obtained during multiple rotation cycles, researchers can determine the amplitude and phase of these periods. A study on the asteroid (10115) 1992 SK, along with (1685) Toro and (1620) Geographos, utilized the YORP constant to calculate the acceleration in angular velocity and the resulting rotation period. For the asteroid (10115) 1992 SK, there is evidence supporting the YORP effect's influence, as is the case with (1685) Toro.

We demonstrate that non-Heisenstein property of a collection of surface group representations is equivalent to the topological compactness of its Topo-character variety under the Rosendal-topology. Additionally, if a collection of surface homeomorphisms is topologically precompact, we prove it must contain a finite number of realizations of distinct semi-simple actions, possibly shifted by commutators of certain curves. Furthermore, if a collection of surface homeomorphisms is non-Topo-precompact, we establish there exists a closed curve whose winding numbers differ by at least 1 for some pairs of homeomorphisms within the collection.

Multiple infinite string comparison techniques have been introduced to overcome limited computability of lexical ordering when applied to infinite strings. This paper formally establishes the framework for synthesizing a wide range of comparison methods operating on infinite strings. It provides proof that a specific class of methods, known as 1-local constructible measures, is sufficient to define computable methods on infinite strings when restricted to strings that are identical up to a certain point. Furthermore, this class of measures is shown to be equivalent to previous works, including the renowned Kolmogorov gauge, while also being shown to offer greater precision than the lexical first-difference measure. Additionally, this paper offers a unique representation for any 1-local constructible measure using the power series of a transition matrix, providing useful properties for further analysis.

In our study, we analyzed the dynamical behavior of an asymmetric, two-
layer heat exchanger model incorporating two gravitating spheres. By examining
several system parameters, we identified various forms of complexity, including
periodic and chaotic states. Notably, in our analysis of the system's global
dynamics, we found multiple "hidden" coexisting attractors under specific ranges
of gravitational strength and milling frequency, as well as in a frequency
milling regime. Moreover, we observed that an asymmetric setting could give rise
to both visible and unseen attractors that could coexist. To further investigate
and distinguish between these "open" and "closed" heat exchanger modes, we
developed an eraser-width metric. Finally, our work provided a comprehensive
analysis of the system's complexity by examining the influence of gravitational
force, milling frequency, and frequency-milling parameter on its dynamics.

To calibrate controllers for safety-critical systems with high precision, it is essential to accurately compute reachable sets, particularly at points where the curvature of the boundary changes. This study aims to enhance the reliability of reachable set calculations by utilizing the Fawzi and Chouman algorithm, which offers efficient convex hull calculations. Building on this foundation, we develop a novel approach to calculate reachable sets, leveraging a second-order method, the Runge-Kutta-Hermite (RKH) algorithm, to minimize the necessity for convex hull calculations. Through numerical tests, it is demonstrated that the new approach produces accurate and computationally efficient results, offering a valuable contribution to the field of control theory.

The animacy organization found in the ventral temporal cortex, a brain region, has been subject to various interpretations with little consensus. Some believe it serves as a foundation for more complex social skills, while others see it as part of a broader biological categorization system or an adaptive trait for prioritizing information. To clarify the nature of this animacy distinction, we used advanced techniques including eye-tracking and neural pattern analysis to compare the representations of living entities, including people, animals, and plants, as well as inanimate objects. Although previous studies suggest that the animacy category is represented differently in the brain than the food-related animacy category, when we used a classifier to distinguish between animate and inanimate images, it became apparent that the ventral temporal cortex's animacy division is indeed essential and cannot be replicated, signifying that the animacy category is indeed "animates vs. non-animates" rather than "animals vs. objects".

The quantum unique ergodicity dilemma attracted the attention of Iwanisew and Tseng, who proposed a revised definition and explored potential solutions. A streamlined approach to their problem is achievable through the utilization of GL(s) elliptic cuts, cutting squares, or Liouville operators restricted to strip domains. A specific aspect of the quantum unique ergodicity problem was addressed by Keating and Rudnick, focusing on the distribution of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function in relation to the critical line. They hypothesized that this anomaly could be attributed to a singular, poorly understood zero of a specific type of Dirichlet character zero. To further investigate, they established that under the assumption of the existence of such a zero, the quantum unique ergodicity problem could be resolved, cutting squares operators would exhibit significant variability, and this would also manifest in other contexts.

We introduce a quantum relational Hoare logic framework that incorporates "expectations" to capture partial correctness assertions for a broad spectrum of quantum programs. This framework expands upon the single-program "expectation" reasoning introduced in recent studies (Alghamdi et al., LIPIC-20). Our work provides a foundation for verifying the partial correctness of a wide range of quantum algorithms, including while loops, conditionals, and composition of programs, and demonstrates the application of this framework to prove partial correctness of prominent quantum algorithms.

The severe persistence of the current COVID-19 pandemic globally can be partly attributed to a significant factor - a small proportion of infected individuals drive a large number of new cases through high transmissibility. This phenomenon, known as a super-spreading event, results from the intersection of biological, environmental, and sociological factors. The primary objective of this study is to examine how a single super-spreading event influences the progression of an epidemic. By utilizing an SIR model and incorporating random variables to determine transmission dynamics, various factors were explored, such as the size of a population, disease lethality, and vital rates. Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations allowed us to derive crucial insights, including the potential for super-spreading events to significantly influence critical metrics like the final number of infected individuals in a population and case-fatality rates. The empirical relevance of these findings is particularly apparent in the ongoing COVID-19 outbreak.

Let V be a complex topological vector space. A subset R of the linear operators on V is termed as a cyclic set of operators on V if the following condition is met: for any non-zero vector x in V, the collection of vectors consisting of x and its transformations under R, denoted as span{x}Rx, is dense in the entire space V. This paper characterizes both single operator tuples and multiple operator tuples that are cyclic sets of operators on any given space, as well as those that are both cyclic sets of operators and have additional properties of being hypercyclic sets of operators. Additionally, it is determined which operators are cyclic sets of operators, which tuples are, and which subsets of operators are, all within the context of the complex topological vector spaces.

The study investigates the presence of bias in inferred vector magnetic field measurements, particularly in images representing line widths. A general, non-asymptotic framework is established to characterize the accuracy of inferred quantities and identify sources of error. A statistical test is proposed to detect the presence of bias, then applied to observational data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory's H-alpha filter. The study reveals that a common approximation used to calculate line width can result in significant bias, comparable to the signal variance. An adjusted estimator is developed to address this issue. The researcher's analysis also explores the assumptions underlying the method's validity.

In order to address this issue, we turned to neural networks to serve as importance samplings, specifically utilizing the Complex Valued Autoregressive Flow network in conjunction with a variational approach to estimate the free energy's projection. To test our model, we used a one-dimensional Hubbard model and found that it could provide reliable results in both neutral and charged scenarios during our simulations.

In today's data-rich world, leveraging existing annotations to train accurate classifiers is commonplace. However, an intriguing opportunity arises when we consider using annotations from unrelated tasks. While previous research has examined simple tasks without related domains, it's essential to explore exploiting annotations from projects with different purposes. To achieve this, our approach targets a specific scenario where the target task shares some features with the source task but is otherwise unrelated. Taking advantage of the abundant data available from such tasks, we've developed an innovative technique known as Retrieval Enhancement (Re). This method automatically identifies and transfers relevant, but not directly transferable, information between the tasks. Through several real-world tests involving a range of tasks, our findings demonstrate that the unique capability of the Re method to generalize across unrelated tasks sets it apart from traditional approaches, with outstanding performance highlighted in the paper's results.

Privacy-preserving machine learning methods, specifically training that is robust to differential privacy, are essential for the secure deployment of deep learning models on sensitive data.  However, evaluating proposed approaches to this challenging problem typically involves significant computational costs, often requiring thousands of repeated calculations on large datasets.  This problem is exacerbated by the necessity of optimizing multiple hyperparameters.  In this work, we introduce HyperOptimized Private Learning (HPRL), an efficient framework for hyperparameter optimization for deep learning models trained with differential privacy.  The HPRL framework utilizes a pre-trained neural network to accurately predict the adjusted learning rate necessary for convergence, eliminating the need for time-consuming trial and error testing.  This approach also removes the learning rate adjustment step from the training process, thereby reducing the computational burden.  The HPRL framework demonstrates superior performance compared to recent learning rate optimization techniques and achieves parities with current state-of-the-art methods while being more efficient in terms of computational resources.

In the context of learning ordered data structures, researchers are examining involutions as a group. Currently, no ordered structure has been established for the complex of involutions, except for the inclusion relationship, in an attempt to define more comprehensive structures. This study implements various ordered structures, including the suffix order, which results in a double ordering when combined with its opposite, and explores the implications of these involutions on educational and biological sequence analysis.

A new statistical approach, based on probabilistic component analysis, has been developed to model stellar populations in galaxies, and its application to the APOGEE-2 dataset reveals key insights.  By comparing results obtained from this method with those from traditional modeling techniques, we found that both approaches yield comparable outcomes when analyzing the Milky Way disk populations with APOGEE spectra.  However, a unique advantage of our method emerges, enabling the identification of subtle population subdivisions and revealing a previously unreported correlation between sodium and titanium.  Furthermore, our analysis highlights nuances in radial and vertical solar circle variations for certain elements and uncovering elements' origins and behaviors through their correlations.

A leading online news website in China published a misleading COVID-19 prevention advice titled "Air purifiers, electrolyte beverages, and face masks are effective; do not buy air tickets and change your travel plans" on March 12, 2020, which gained significant attention on WeChat Public Accounts. Our analysis of the spread of this rumor among Chinese users revealed a new mechanism called the "spread chain," consisting of four key components: major platforms, influential accounts, cross-platform sharing, and high-frequency exposure accounts. Among the major platforms, entertainment-related platforms offered wider coverage, while health-related platforms provided more precise targeting. In addition to platform influence, the type of account that shares the rumor also impacts its spread, with government and judicial accounts having the highest ability to stop the spread, followed by educational accounts. Our research identified the main channels of rumor transmission as domestic travel (31.8%), followed by work-related (25.3%) and community settings (13.3). To further examine the spread of the rumor across different age groups, we conducted in-depth interviews with 40 participants and found that younger users were more susceptible to sharing the rumor due to their higher frequency of social media usage. Our study offers a comprehensive understanding of the spread chain of online rumors and identifies the main settings of interpersonal communication in China, providing valuable insights for future prevention and mitigation efforts.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies within the Fornax cluster involves examining local planetary nebulae within them. As the spectral analysis of these objects advances, precise distance measurements become achievable through the examination of [O III] nebular lines, providing insights into the geometry of planetary nebulae and ultimately helping to determine the distance to the galaxies they reside in. To apply this method effectively, it is essential to obtain high-resolution spectra from a large number of planetary nebulae within the same galaxies. With the utilization of the 4D-SLDS code, an extensive search was conducted using Pan-STARRS1 data to identify suitable candidates within the central region of the Fornax cluster, encompassing four galaxies (AM 1, AM 2, SOGGI, and AMG 1). To further refine this list, additional criteria such as apparent brightness limits based on absolute magnitude and metallicity considerations were applied, resulting in a curated planetary nebulae directory for these galaxies. Furthermore, measurements of the distance modulus to each galaxy were obtained through the analysis of the width of the [O III] lines, although results to some extent show discrepancies likely attributed to non-spherical symmetry of the nebulae, highlighting the need to evaluate alternative theoretical models. The rise in IoT devices and mobile applications has created a high demand for real-time flow analysis systems, making performance a critical factor for developers. Currently, generic flow analysis tools like SQL and Raol fail to deliver the required performance, while high-performance alternatives are often too specialized, limiting their versatility. To overcome these limitations, we propose Rafters, a performance-optimized flow processing engine that retains the flexibility of a generic engine. Rafters incorporates a novel interpretive technique called bytecode caching to enhance performance. In addition to caching frequently used parts of the flow graph, Rafters converts optimized sections into a native instruction set. To further improve performance for recurring flow graphs, we've developed Raflow, a static optimizer that transforms periodic streams into a high-performance version of Rafters. Evaluations using the Raflow toolkit demonstrate a significant performance improvement of up to 28x over non-real-time engines and 33x to 400x over specialized real-time engines. The performance gains achieved by Rafters and Raflow can be considered crucial for effective flow analysis in IoT and mobile environments.

A specific type of curve in a higher-dimensional space, called a timelike Bertrand curve, is being investigated in relation to the underlying geometric properties of a $(2,n)$-dimensional semi-Euclidean environment. The paper establishes that timelike curves, known as Riemannian Bertrand curves in Euclidean space, cannot exist within semi-Euclidean spaces when limited to certain lower-dimensional configurations. Furthermore, clear conditions under which timelike Bertrand curves can exist in these settings are derived. Additionally, the concept of timelike W-fourth order Bertrand curves is defined and characterized within the semi-Euclidean framework.

The choice of loss function in classification tasks is a critical decision that directly influences a deep neural network's performance. Although commonly used loss functions such as softmax with cross-entropy are the norm, there is no in-depth understanding of how other, less conventional loss functions, could also be effectively utilized. This report investigates a broad spectrum of 55 loss functions, aiming to provide a guiding framework for selecting appropriate loss functions for classification tasks. Furthermore, it explores the implications of loss function choices on the probability distributions generated by deep neural networks.

This research aims to advance the simulation of thermomechanical changes in polymer crystallization triggered by strain. Understanding the underlying mechanisms of strain-induced crystallization in polymers necessitates a coupled simulation of thermal, mechanical, and structural processes. To effectively accelerate numerical simulations of these changes, particularly during the nucleation stage, we developed a simplified model that skips the need for stochastic nucleation simulation. Instead, we incorporated a double-nucleated state with associated crystalline nuclei density into the set of balance and rate equations. A novel equation for crystalline nuclei density decay, along with modified nucleation density equations, was derived to prevent unrealistic growth. To manage the vast difference in time scales of nucleation and crystal growth, an efficient and stable numerical solver utilizing implicit-explicit methods was devised. This solver employs selective time-step application, allowing for more accurate simulation with significantly reduced computational cost. The resulting model demonstrates a realistic simulation of strain-induced crystallization evolution in polymers.

To better fully describe the paramagnetic response to an external magnetic field applied perpendicular to a nematic superconductor's symmetry plane, a theoretical framework was developed. Analytical expressions for the magnetic response can be derived within the Fumi gas model. Furthermore, this approach allows us to incorporate the impact of superconductor thickness. Computational results show that the magnetic response to an infinite thickness superconductor can be directly applied to thin-film samples. Additionally, we discovered that for perpendicular magnetic fields, the Pauli paramagnetic response of Cooper pairs in the triplet state is a crucial component. This is in contrast to Type-I and Anderson triplet states, where the Pauli response of Cooper pairs is negligible.

A newly proposed differential continuous-phase modulation (CPM) detection method, which allows for a greater delay in a matched filter, is analyzed in depth. The investigation compares various detection methods, both coherent and non-coherent, for a 2-Dinary modulated signal with raised cosine filtering, resulting in the creation of an extensive library of detection impulse responses for reference. The analysis explores multiple aspects, including the bandwidth requirements, the complexity of implementation, and the statistical properties, in an effort to determine whether the proposed delay enhancement can be practically applied. The results indicate that increasing the matched filter delay from one symbol period to two periods offers a significant benefit, and that equivalent performance can be achieved either with improved matched filter delay or reduced rolling window length. The analysis also reveals that this approach provides better detection properties than the conventional non-coherent differential CPM method.

A previous theory of spacetime quantum compressibility, initially developed for cold reservoirs, has been adapted to consider thermal reservoirs at a specific temperature. This adaptation demonstrates that spacetime quantum compressibility equates to quantum capacity, confirming that it remains constant with temperature in cold reservoirs but becomes thermal in nature at higher temperatures. Specifically, there's a transition transition occurrence around the Hubble temperature, demonstrating that compressibility loses its quantum aspect above this temperature. The application of this theory indicates that spacetime cannot act as a quantum engine at temperatures exceeding the Hubble temperature, thus limiting the minimum feasible temperature to approximately $10^{-29}$ K. Theoretical framework extends to bosonic fields, showing that for these fields, compressibility becomes thermal at temperatures exceeding a fraction of the Hubble temperature.

The emergence of large language models with powerful natural language understanding capabilities has been accompanied by criticism of their limited reasoning skills. The foundation of propositional reasoning, crucial for more advanced reasoning types, relies on the "if-then" operator, yet evaluations involving this conditional statement have been historically underutilized. We introduce ATOMIC, an extensive dataset comprising 15,000 reasoning problems based on the "if-then" statement, which integrates diverse statements, sources, and complexities. We further conduct both human-based logical consistency checks and associational analyses to examine how natural reasoning connects to model performance. Our findings reveal that models' reasoning prowess is hindered by associative statements and longer passages, while human-stated prior knowledge significantly influences correct answer prediction.

A significant body of research suggests that quantum computing algorithms, including those for optimization and machine learning, can effectively handle the limitations of noisy quantum hardware. This S.P.O.I.L.E.R. project takes an innovative approach by applying a quantum variant of hybrid Monte-Carlo simulation to accelerate financial portfolio optimization on actual, near-term quantum computing devices. Rather than relying purely on classical methods or quantum-machine learning hybrids, this work embraces a quantum-classical combination. It leverages the HHL quantum solver to accelerate the Monte-Carlo component of portfolio optimization. The research compares three distinct implementations - a basic HHL version, an amplified HMOA (a quantum-enhanced hybrid method) version, and a standard HMMOCKL (a classical mock liquidity version) - to evaluate their performance. Through extensive simulations and real-world testing using the IBM Quantum Computer, the HHL and HMOAD clusters demonstrate notable portfolio optimization speedups. Notably, the HMMOCKL method outperforms the HHL cluster in specific time windows, highlighting the importance of tailored tuning to maximize the benefits of quantum computing in real-world applications.

To enhance data efficiency and speech recognition accuracy, a new training method called "Bidirectional Multi-Modal Attention (MuAtt)" is proposed, allowing the model to automatically identify and prioritize matching speech and text data while filtering out mismatched pairs. The model is built using a transformer architecture and BERT components, incorporating modules that encode both unimodal and multi-modal information, and a multi-task objective that guides the speech-text matching process and natural language understanding. The MuAtt model is further extended with an end-to-end speech recognition loss, and through ablation studies, it is demonstrated that the MuAtt model not only streamlines training but also outperforms the strong baseline model on speech understanding and natural language processing. Additionally, it is shown that the MuAtt model facilitates a comprehensive analysis of speech representations and recovers missing text information more effectively than current models.
